source_text: Verum quia et in primo et in praesenti certamine, argumentatione Augustini claruit non esse eum Traducianorum Deum, quem Christiani iustum atque omnium conditorem concinenti assertione venerantur; praecipio iam animo, quo plurimi eorum quoque, qui caeco errore lapsi sunt, his agnitis corrigantur.
pass_a_gloss: But because both in the first and in the present contest, by Augustine's argumentation it became clear that he is not the God of the Traducians, whom Christians venerate by a harmonious assertion as just and founder of all; I already command in my mind that very many even of those who have fallen by a blind error, these things having been recognized, may be corrected.

lemmas.lexica: Julian's polemic label for teachers of tradux peccati
LS tradux=vine-shoot/layer; Blaise tradux peccati=transmission of sin by descent
LS conditor; Blaise God as maker from nothing

pass_b_english: But both in the earlier dispute and in the present one, Augustine’s argument has made clear that the god of those who teach inherited sin is not the God whom Christians, with one voice, worship as just and as the creator of all things. I already anticipate in my mind that many even of those who fell through blind error will correct themselves once they recognize this.

choices.why: Julian's polemic target is inherited sin as a natural evil (malum naturale), the vine-layer metaphor, not a later systematic 'original sin' slogan and not soul-traducianism as such.
rejected: original sin (later system as default gloss)
traducianism of the soul (not the load here)

choices.why: Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
